text_fidelity_a:
Pentax K100D Super 6.1MP Digital SLR Camera Shake Reduction and 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Lens First of all, I would like to start with highly recommending this camera to ANYONE who wants premium image quality with expandability, power and flexibility.

Pentax is one of the only companies out there that is driven entirely by photography and NOT by a marketing department that makes outrageous claims. To this end, even this, their lowest-end camera, is PACKED with premium features. Let's take a look at them:

1. Dust Reduction: Dust WILL get into your camera! This keeps it off of the sensor and increases the time inbetween cleanings.

2. Shake Reduction: It's good for a couple of stops of shooting leeway and you get it with every lens you use. Other companies build their systems into the lenses, meaning ONE lens can cost as much or more than the camera, itself! Lens-based anti-shake systems are more effective at long zoom than body-based systems, but unless you're rich, you won't be able to afford a suite of good lenses! With this camera, you can use ANY Pentax lens and get anti-shake.

3. AA batteries: Proprietary battery packs are NO GOOD. Hmmm, if you're on a shoot and your pack dies, you're not taking ANY photos unless you get a spare, right? With this camera, pick up some 2500mAh Ni-MH AA's and you can afford to get three sets. However, the power drain is so small, you might not need more than one set.

4. 6 MP sensor: Don't EVER get trapped in the megapixel hype. Megapixels mean nothing in the DSLR game, except for noise issues. Let me explain. The sensor sizes on almost all DSLRs (except for $5000 full-frame pro cameras) are APS-sized, meaning the sensor size on this camera and the Nikon D300 are very nearly the same dimensions. This means that photosensors on the chip have to be made smaller to get more pixels...meaning that the closer together/smaller sites are LESS light sensitive and they will also interfere with each other. 6 MP is a perfect sweet spot for noise and image sharpness. You get a base ISO of 200, meaning your camera is TWICE as sensitive to light as one with a base ISO of 100! This camera records color accurately and makes prints up to 8.5"x11" with no problem.

This camera has huge features and, even with the release of the K20D and K200D cameras, still maintains a good feature/image quality set with a proven CCD sensor and a suite of easy-to-learn features and settings. I LOVE this camera and even though I have a K200D for the weather sealing and larger burst capacity, the K100D super is the camera I ALWAYS take with me in trips. You're better off getting this camera plus a really nice lens and a 360FZ flash than a more expensive camera with a base kit lens and no external flash.

Believe me, this camera's quality will not fail to impress you and it will grow with you. It can use ANY lens its bigger brothers can and it uses them effortlessly.

A superb camera and one for the record books!
text_fidelity_b: Pentax K100D Super 6.1MP Digital SLR Camera Shake Reduction and 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Lens

Amazon Basics Campus Backpack for Laptops up to 15-Inches - Green I'm often surprised at what you can get for $10 as even the chinese branded junk is cheaply made is unsubstantial at a higher price point. This backpack has cavernous capacity, good zippers, pocket diversity, and is padded like a Timbuk2 (though not armored like one). It is also lightweight for such a substantial pack. I can't comment on durability as only time will tell but the zipper pulls don't feel like cheap pot metal that will break after a few weeks. It also is non-descript and not laden with stupid junk like MOLLE/PALS webbing or two dozen straps and shock cords. Sternum strap stays out of the way until needed. No belt strap (which is good), and lots and lots of space. This has become my favorite work backpack and carries everything I need and more.

My only wish for this one would be zipper pulls that have eyelets so I can string paracord loops for pull extensions. Otherwise fives all around.

UPDATE (9/9/2021): I still use this everyday. I have two other Timbuk2s and another similar pack from eBags, as well as a number of very useful packs from Dakine and Camelbak. You can probably tell I like bags. This little $10 backpack carries more, is just as durable, can go in the washing machine (put it in a large mesh bag to wash), and is very comfortable. I almost need an excuse to use one of the other more expensive bags. Also, no zipper issues, no fraying, no tears or loose threads.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Campus Backpack for Laptops up to 15-Inches - Green

text_fidelity_a:
3DConnexion 3DX-700059 Spacemouse Compact 3D Mouse At first I was skeptical about the idea of using my left hand for this. I was initially expecting it to be a replacement mouse for my right hand, but after more research I understood what they are trying to do. I must say that it's much easier to use than I expected, and operating it with my left hand works just fine.

I was also hesitant because of the price. However, this mouse is fantastic. Worth every penny. I'm using it with SketchUp, and it's vastly easier and faster than the normal built-in navigation tools. It's hard to articulate just how awesome this is. Once you get used to it, it's instinctive and effortless, and moving around the model is so easy! You will absolutely love it.

There was one tricky thing during the setup, however. I plugged it in, loaded the driver, and launched SketchUp. Then I found and opened the configuration window to customize it for SketchUp. The info I had found showed that configuration window with "SketchUp" at the top, and the SketchUp-specific options. But my configuration window didn't have anything specific to SketchUp. It said Windows Explorer at the top instead of SketchUp. I thought I was missing a driver. I messed around a log time, and looked through lots of online info.

At one point, I noticed it said Chrome instead of Windows Explorer. That's when I figured it out. The configuration window changes by itself, based on what application is active. I had SketchUp running in the background, but my most recent activity was with Windows Explorer and then Chrome. With the configuration window open, I clicked over into the SketchUp window, and suddenly the configuration window said SketchUp at the top, and the the SketchUp-specific settings appeared. I wish that had been in the instructions somewhere!!

At first I didn't bother programming the buttons, but later I tried it, and that's an awesome feature. For Sketchup, I programmed one button to be "remove guides", and the other is "paste in place". Hitting those buttons is much faster than finding those things in the menu each time. However, I discovered that I need to make sure I'm not moving through the model when I press the "paste in place" button, or the mouse locks up, and I need to restart SketchUp. But as long as I make sure I'm not moving when I press it, I never have that problem anymore.

Anyway, you will absolutely love this. After using it, I no longer had any doubt about it being worth the money. It's worth every penny. I would give it 6 stars if I could.
text_fidelity_b: 3DConnexion 3DX-700059 Spacemouse Compact 3D Mouse

text_fidelity_a:
Motorola T200TP Talkabout Radio, 3 Pack This is a nice little set of radios, improved from my last three-pack of similarly priced Motorolas, but has some room for improvement.

Goods:

+ Good size - small enough, but big enough to fit in your hand comfortably like a radio should. Yes, it could be smaller, but at some point you don't really want smaller.

+ Some basic options to customize, mostly the noises the radios make. LCD screen shows you what you need to know.

+ Batteries can be charged while in the radios via standard Micro USB adapters - two are included. One charges one radio while the other charges two simultaneously.

+ Belt clip included. Head sets can be added.

Bad:

- While it's great that the battery packs can be charged via USB and the chargers are accepted worldwide (whereas my previous set for work had barrel connections to the charger and I burnt one out the first night I tried to charge due to being in Europe, the battery/charger setup is still imperfect for two reasons:

1) Battery packs are not three separate batteries that could be charged with other chargers and switched with other batteries (think Eneloop). My Garmin topo GPS came with actual rechargeable batteries that could be used elsewhere. This makes sense when you want to be able to carry standard alkaline batteries for emergencies/backup. These battery packs are great that they can be replaced with AA when necessary, but not as good as standard, replaceable rechargeable batteries (but you can use rechargeable batteries as your backup batteries).

2) N-MH doesn't make sense for this application because these are the type of batteries that develop a "memory". If you use these every day for work, then you want to recharge them every night. Actually, you would be inclined to recharge every time you want to use them, period, to be sure you get the most from the batteries. But because of the memory, you really want to discharge them fully. The appropriate type of battery would be Li-ion, because they would be chargeable every night AND would last longer. This is the biggest negative to this rig. If the battery packs were Li-ion, I would not care that they are packs versus separate batteries.

- Belt clip should be taken off to remove battery cover without beating the two up. This is apparently an obvious issue to the manufacturer because they have a protective piece of plastic between the two for shipment.

Neutral (strange):

Two standard USB chargers included, at 500mA output each (1A would be minimum standard and expected these days, but whatever; they may have done this to avoid overcharging overnight). Both have the same rated input, but the output is the same (samex2 on the 2 output charger). That actually doesn't make sense, unless the single charger is half as efficient (or they are just too lazy to change the nameplate). Not really sure what's up with that, but I sort of like the 2-output charger. I expect most people have so many USB chargers laying around that they'll use whatever is at hand anyway vice these.
text_fidelity_b: Motorola T200TP Talkabout Radio, 3 Pack

I can't speak to how it works in modes other than repeater, but given it's excellent repeater functionality, I would imagine other modes work just as well.

With the exception of the instructions, zero problems with this. It’s a very effective (and compact) solution to extending WiFi coverage. Highly recommend.

JVC HAECX20B Sports Clip Inner Ear Headphones, Black The sound quality of these earbuds AKA headphones is excellent. They are exactly what they are advertised to be, earbuds with clips that go over the ears to keep them from falling out of your ears when you are engaged in activities that cause a lot of moving and shaking of your head, which would dislodge ordinary earbuds.

I don't personally engage in sports that strenuous, but but I did thoroughly test these Sports Clips by bending over, hopping up and down and generally moving my head a lot. They did not come loose from my ears.

I found another excellent use for them as well. When I have normal earbuds plugged in when I am baking bread or other dishes that get my hands very messy, all too frequently non-clip earbuds begin to slip out of my ears. Its a real pain to have to wash sticky dough off my hands and dry them before I can stuff the loose earbuds back into my ears. I don't have that problem at all with these Sports Clips earbuds, and that's very convenient.

The one flaw with this product, at least it's a flaw to me, because it doesn't make any sense and is somewhat uncomfortable, is the way the cord is designed. It is not coequal in length on both sides. One side is about four times longer than the other. There also isn't any sliding plastic piece that allows you to adjust the length of the splitting of the cord so that the user can adjust how wide it gaps over one's throat and chest, which would allow the user to opt, as desired, to even tighten it right up under the chin.

Other than those issues, this is an excellent product.

text_fidelity_a:
Everstone Adjustable Tilt TV Wall Mount Bracket for Most 32-90 Inch LED,LCD,OLED,Plasma Flat Screen,Curved TVs,Low Profile,Up to VESA 600x400 and 165 lbs,Fits 16",18",24" First let me get the positive out of the way. Very easy to assemble, sturdy, and I like the fact that I can secure the TV on the wall by the top as well as pop it free by unlocking the unit by pulling the two chains s on the bottom. It was very easy to assemble, and I like the fact that they gave you a leveler to make sure its straight. The images I posted is a 75-inch TV, the maximum it can hold is apparently an 80. However, the bigger you go, the harder it gets to reach behind the back to tilt it. There is still 2 1/2 space to run wires and reach around to turn the knob to tilt it forward or backwards.

Now the CON.

I was not planning on tilting this unit forward or backwards because it's a big tv. For those looking for a decent mount and plan on doing the exact same thing having it flat, with a little space behind it so that you can reach around and run the wires the two inches and a half for me of space was perfect. I secured the tilting mechanism to keep it facing forward. which are the two metal knobs as you see in my second uploaded image as well as Amazon's version in the photos. I figured that since it had two turning knobs it was the same as the previous one I owned that had a spinning knob that went forward unlock, and backwards lock. I installed some LED lights on the back of the TV and hung it on the mount 1 month later. However I decided to remove the LED lights on the unit without taking the whole TV off the wall because I can easily take those off by just pulling the lights off.

This is where the problem started and noticed the manufacturing or designer error, hopefully they can correct it in the future. When I pulled the LED off, it tilted the TV slightly upwards, no idea why when it was apparently secured facing forward when I tried reaching around to the side to turn the nob I noticed the little ball fell out of the turning metal nob. The ball that goes into the metal unit was super glued on and it's not a turning ball where you can put it in there, screw in to permanently secure it in place to metal rod.

This created a problem when I wanted to tilt the TV forward, I had to move the metal rod because now the ball fell off it and it could not be attached again because it was held in place by super glue when you turn the knob, the whole unit would slide through falling off. Also if you notice in the picture, it's three separate parts. Not only was the metal rod with the ball superglued on but the unit that you used to turn in place unscrews off because there's no resistance or warning mechanism when you're turning the knob you don't know which way to turn to tilt it.

Since I was trying to figure out which way to make it go forward and backwards I realized that the whole unit was unscrewing because I could keep turning it in a direction until the whole metal rod as well as the screw / nob came completely off. This means that I now had to reattach it back to the unit screw it back in as well as dealing with the ball that had fallen off the stick. I ended up just removing both of them and physically moving the TV by hand forward and upwards luckily it didn't require a lot of force and it must have been slightly loose.

Regardless of all that I would still recommend the unit. It is sturdy it's nice and I like the adequate space behind it or I can reach around the problem is that if you have a big TV and you plan on constantly tilting it forward and backwards before attaching it on the wall. it's probably better for you to tilt the TV and then attach it to the wall because reaching around the 75 inch TV it's a little bit more difficult easier to run a wire because you have more than enough space but harder if you want to reach the handle to tilt it forward and backwards.

Also in the setup video instructions, it's simply rotates the nob without saying counterclockwise lock, counterclockwise relock etc etc. There's also no resistance mechanism that would tell you it can't go forward. So what ends up happening is that you can unscrew the whole nob bar off by mistake leaving the screw on the mount and nob in your hand. Hopefully in a future revision. The one thing I've noticed is that nearby electrical devices, and especially ones with motors in them, will definitely throw this extender for a loop. We have an air purifier that lived first next to this extender, and then at a point about five feet from the extender, but between the extender and the router, and the extender did not like either of those situations at all. Lots of orange-light action (an orange light on this extender means no wifi signal). Moved the air purifier well away from the extender and out of the signal path and all was hunky-dory again.

I'm geeky sometimes and would like to be able to log onto the extender and muck with settings or at least make sure everything's good beyond what the green light tells me, but I don't seem to be able to do that once the extender's been set up; I can only get to the setup/configuration page after resetting the extender using the button on the back. But I'll live. The extender seems to be doing what we expect of it, and that's...all we expect of it (funny how that works).
text_fidelity_b: Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310

Bluetooth Headphones for iPhone - Green I see people raving up and down about the perfection and wonderfulness of these headphones; I’m not as completely blown away by them as those people are. Quality of construction does seem to be excellent (although because Amazon doesn’t lower all prices at the start of Prime Day but only lowers some of them well after Prime Day has begun, I had to send back the first pair I bought and purchase another pair to get a discounted price, and the piston things for extending and compressing the size of the headphones was smoother on the first pair I had) and they’re comfortable enough to wear for extended periods, but while it may be a limitation of Bluetooth (I don’t know), I haven’t noticed myself being amazed by their bass response. No, in fact I just now watched the video for Shake It Off and listened to a couple of Lana Del Rey tracks and these headphones are definitely lacking in bass response – as in, there’s very little, and what there is gets completely lost under any midrange and high-end sounds that may be playing at the same time. They’re tinny-sounding. I have to wonder what the people are listening to with these who are praising the sound quality so enthusiastically.

On the other hand, I don’t ordinarily listen to music anymore, but only to talks and lectures; While I’m watching movies is probably the only time I’m going to really want big bass, and I watched The Revenant last night and didn’t feel like I was missing anything…

So their construction is much more solid than that of probably most other headphones on the market, they’re comfortable to wear, and there’s a nice ecosystem of accessories out there, but I personally find the sound quality quite lacking and I’m going to have to decide whether to hang onto these or return them.

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle, 6" E Ink Display, Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) I'm a big fan of Kindle e-Readers. We own two of the older generation ones (the last Kindles with keyboard) and for x-mas I bought my mother a Kindle Fire HD 8.9 for x-mas. But, alas, she doesn't seem to have fine enough motor control to hit the small buttons on that device (see my review for that device). So the Fire has been sitting unused on the coffee table for a few months now.

But this is not a review of the Fire HD 8.9. I want to describe my very short experience with the basic Kindle and the Kindle Paperwhite - as they relate to the intended user: my mom. She recently suffered a stroke and one of the side effects is that she now has a constant tremble in her left hand. As she had trouble with the Fire HD 8.9 we went to Staples to see if the more purpose-built Kindles were easier to operate. We were not surprised when she often made mistakes selecting books on the Paperwhite's touch screen. But we were surprised to find that she couldn't even handle the physical buttons on the basic Kindle! From what I could tell, the problems were: the side-buttons (page forward/backward) are much smaller and narrower than they were on our old Kindles (which my mom had no trouble with), so basic navigation among pages became iffy. Similarly, the D-pad is smaller too - and that made selection of books difficult for her. Finally, while I could easily hold my old Kindle with one hand AND operate the page forward button, this is a bit more difficult with the new basic Kindle. My mom could not manage it at all. And since she can't hold the Kindle with her trembling left hand, neither e-Reader was for her. [She is now making do with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9 by laying it on a flat surface and only operating it with her right hand].

I'm still giving the Kindle 4 stars because none of these shortcomings are of interest to the majority of people, but I wanted folks to be aware of the newer devices' potential limitations with those suffering from limited motor skills.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle, 6" E Ink Display, Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)

text_fidelity_a: Tenda Wi-Fi Dual Band range extender Let me start by saying I am just a layman so I can’t go into technical issues about this router, if there are any. But I can tell you, as an average person, I love this router. I am using this in lieu of the FIOS router they tried to force on me. it also replaces a pricier TP Link router that failed miserably after 2 weeks. I wanted to be able to cover as much of my house as possible and IF possible eliminate the WiFi extender. This router does that. When I had FIOS installed the line was put in my living room downstairs on the furthest away spot. Great for my entertainment area terrible for my upstairs office on the other side of the house. Which is why I needed an extender for my computer. Now my computer gets almost full signal strength and phenomenal speed. Since my computer only works on 2.4 band speed sucked. With this router I am very close to my 100/100 FIOS speed on the computer! Very happy. Another thing I’ve noticed: when i tried to play 4K content on my TV it constantly buffered. No more. I have been watching 4K with NO issues not even a stutter. Not only do I find the signal strong it is robust enough to handle all my devices (smart electric plugs, blink cameras, computer, phone my Echo and Ech Dot, etc) and it wants more. There’s nothing weak about this router. As for the cons: setup was time consuming. Not impossible but it wasn’t intuitive. I got it done in less than 1/2 an hour but it could have been quicker. The user interface is decent. There are a lot of options. Heck you can even choose the signal strength for each band, and you can set up a VPN. Previously I had to use DD-WRT to do that. Not now. What makes me even happier? The price! Under $60 and I got one heck of a router. I think the material is what I would expect. So no disappointment there. As you see by my pictures my 5.0 band is what I have always gotten: the speed I pay for. BUT my 2.4 signal is much much better (close to the 100 mb I buy) than it had been using “name brand”’routers. I am very pleased I bit the bullet and bought this. I almost didn’t because it’s not a name I know and some reviews were less than glowing. For me this works great and I hope if you buy it you too are pleased.
text_fidelity_b: Tenda Wi-Fi Dual Band range extender

text_fidelity_a:
Tiffen 82VND 82 Millimeter Variable ND Filter Shooting video outdoors with a DSLR requires, obviously, proper exposure. When shooting at 24 (23.978) frames per second, the normal shutter speed should be 1/50th of a second (1/60 at 29.97 fps). If the camera is set at the lowest ISO rating of 100, in bright daylight the f/stop would be around f/22. If you want to operate at wider aperture to achieve shallow depth of field, you need to cut the light.

This variable density filter allows such an adjustment. The problem is that it cuts the light by rotating two polarizing filters against each other. Polarizers can be tricky and, by design, modify the quality of light. Thus it may act unexpectedly.

One downside is that the front of the filter is not threaded and my 77mm model is a larger diameter than the 70-200mm Nikon zoom it fits on. So now the bayonet lens hood won't fit. Now I'm outdoors with a filter on the lens and no hood to block flare. There aren't any hoods that naturally fit the filter so you need to tape a hood to the outer ring or use a matte box.
text_fidelity_b: Tiffen 82VND 82 Millimeter Variable ND Filter

Macbook Pro Charger 96W Usb-C Power Adapter For Macbook Pro Air 13 14 15 16 Inch Mac Book Retina M2 M1 2022 2021 2020 2019 2018 2017 2016 Usb-C To C Fast Charging Charger For IPad Pro/All USB C Device My laptop came with a Dell PA1900-02D (9T215) which I still have and works fine. I wanted a second charger for another location. The EasyStyle SK90B195462looks like the original but is much lighter, probably due to being a switching power supply. My laptop had been discharged down to 5% prior to plugging the replacement charger in. The connector fit fine, but the laptop did not recognize the charger and warned that it may not work. I figured that's just Dell telling me it's not a Dell accessory. I permanently shut off the warning (an option) and continued to use the EasyStyle charger. Charging appeared normal and battery status was indicated as charging. However, after a short while it seemed stuck at 11% charge. I came back a few hours later and it was still indicating at 11%. I plugged in the Dell charger and 100% full charge was indicated immediately. I unplugged the Dell charger and the computer still indicated nearly full charge. I plugged in the new EasyStyle charger and the indication was charging and still near full charge.
My conclusion is that the charger works, but may cause the computer to give incorrect charge status under some conditions and it will be best to unplug the charger to get an accurate battery status.

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Galaxy Tab (7-inch, 16GB, Wi-Fi) I really liked this 7" Tab (GT-P1010) at first. It's most useful function is web surfing.

Now, after several months of use, it's SLOOOOOOOW to load and update pages and locks up occasionally for no particular reason. I've uninstalled every unnecessary app but whether using the default Browser or Dolphin, it's more frustrating than useful.

It's also inaccurate for when inputting via keyboard. Oftentimes the keyboard adds wild characters all by itself.

Forget firmware updates. You are stuck with whatever it came with. And if you think Samsung will be any help, think again. I put "GT-P1010" in Samsung's product support page and got "no results."

I have to say Apple's major firmware updates work a whole lot better. First, because they happen at all and second, because they are seamless and reliable. Android is buggy and needs fixing on this Samsung Tablet. Samsung's "answer" is to buy a new tablet.

The device has two cameras and would be ideal for video chatting, but won't work with Skype. Apparently it needs the next version of Android. (See above concerning that impossibility.) But who knows if the next-up model will work either?

These things all want to be Apple but simply fall short.

One nice thing is that most Flash content is supported when web surfing. Apple is way lacking here. I used an iPad 1 for some time and it's pretty frustrating that it simply ignores so much content.

Bottom line is I won't buy another wannabe Samsung device like this that lacks firmware updates. (I did the same thing looking for the perfect mp3 player: everyone tried to sell the "iPod killer" and I spent more money trying to avoid the iPod. Then I bought an iPod3 and later an iPhone4 and understood how excellent their engineering and software and OS are and how with OS updates the devices continually get better even after you make the purchase.) They are too expensive to throw away and Samsung can't or won't fix the bugs. Thus you are stuck with an expensive, buggy toy that's frustrating to use. No thank you.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy Tab (7-inch, 16GB, Wi-Fi)

ZHIWHIS Shortwave Radio, MP3 Player with Weather Radios Portable AM FM, Retro Bluetooth Speaker with 6 EQ Modes, Rechargeable Alarm Clock Receiver with Sleep Time and NOAA Alerts ZWS-701 I now own two emergency types of radios, this one, and another. This means I can compare this to something directly. The following are the reasons why I like this radio more than the other:

1). It’s TINY. It can fit in the front pocket of your shirt or jacket.

2). It’s analogue. This old fashioned tuning style happens to be my preference for radios. It is simple, and you have more control in tuning into the exact radio station that you want without hassle.

3). This radio comes equipped with an antenna extension that includes what appears to be a copper coil. So if you can’t get good reception with this radio’s built in antenna, out comes this Tesla-esque looking attachment!

4). It is yellow jacket yellow. It won’t get so easily lost in the clutter, if you choose not to use it unless hazardous weather conditions are reported.

Now: things that I like less about this radio:

1). It isn’t water resistant/ waterproof

2). For the money, I think that an extra feature or two could be added. For the same price, I also have an emergency radio that has solar panels, reading lamp, compass, an SOS alarm, flashlight, a hand crank, and provides a powered docking station for my devices in case of a power outage.

But to each their own. Perhaps those reading this review aren’t interested in owning an emergency radio that is a transformer. Maybe you want to keep things simple, and are not as enamored of gadgets as I. Regardless of which radio you ultimately go with, and this one is great for size and analogue tuning, you should always keep it charged up and use it frequently enough during non emergency times that you will fully understand how it functions and not be taken by surprise by a random power outage.
text_fidelity_b: ZHIWHIS Shortwave Radio, MP3 Player with Weather Radios Portable AM FM, Retro Bluetooth Speaker with 6 EQ Modes, Rechargeable Alarm Clock Receiver with Sleep Time and NOAA Alerts ZWS-701

Razer Kraken BT Kitty Edition: Bluetooth 5.0-40ms Low Latency Connection - Custom-Tuned 40mm Drivers - Beamforming Microphone - Powered Chroma - Quartz Pink The Razer Kraken BT Kitty headset is not a serious gaming headset. The lighting effects and cat ears look cool, and it’s Bluetooth so no wires like the original Kraken Kitty -- those are the big pros.

Razer Synapse does not recognize the headset, so if you want to customize it, two different phone apps are needed.

The Razer Chroma RGB app handles lighting options. The Razer Audio app handles sound settings, firmware updates, and changing the auto shutoff timer.

Do I really want to use my phone to manage my gaming headset? No. I consider having to use my phone while I’m playing a game on my computer to be a hassle!

I did find that I could customize the lighting effects with my phone, unpair the headphones from my phone and then pair them with my computer to keep the lighting effects while using with my computer. But that is also a hassle, considering Razer has a program meant to handle this!

Sound quality is just okay -- it’s not great. I’m not an audiophile so it works for me, but I have less expensive headphones that have better playback, even to my inexperienced ears. The headphones do not have ANC and I miss that a lot.

The controls are basic, a volume wheel and a power button. The power button can be used to pause and play, just hold it in for two seconds and let go, and the music will pause. Hold in for two seconds and let go to resume.

The headphones don’t have a 3.5mm audio jack, they are only Bluetooth. The charging cable is micro USB.

I have the Kraken Kitty wired headset, and I wanted a wireless version because once I started using Bluetooth headphones, I couldn’t stand being chained at my desk by a wire. But I feel like Razer wanted to appeal to women gamers -- make it pink, slap on kitty ears -- and didn’t focus as much on quality or function.
text_fidelity_b: Razer Kraken BT Kitty Edition: Bluetooth 5.0-40ms Low Latency Connection - Custom-Tuned 40mm Drivers - Beamforming Microphone - Powered Chroma - Quartz Pink

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra SUPREME Driver's Edition Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging - Black/Silver I've been resistant for quite some time to using a bluetooth device however recent laws have made it impossible not to have one. And it certainly didn't help hearing friends complain about the problems they had with their bluetooth units.

This is really easy to set up. First you activate the bluetooth on your phone (in my case an Iphone 4), then you open up the Jabra Supreme boom to turn it on and at that point it should automatically enter into a pairing mode with your phone and a blue light will appear on the boom. You should see the device name pop up on your phone as Jabra Supreme, then a voice in your ear will say "connected" and you're set to go. Couldn't be simpler.

It fits very comfortably over my ear even with a baseball cap on and sunglasses. The package also comes with a headphone attachment in case this suits you better. I'm able to hear conversations and respond with total clarity even when I'm driving with the top down in my car. There's also a voice command feature which allows you to redial, call back or activate certain phone commands in a total hands-free environment. And for additional features you can download the available app.

Charging the Jabra Supreme is as simple as either plugging into a USB port or using an AC charger. Battery indicator flashes green while charging and then goes out when it's fully loaded - approximately 2 hours later.

This is a terrific little device. In fact, this may cause me more problems as in the past I was always reluctant to talk on the phone while driving. Not anymore.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra SUPREME Driver's Edition Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging - Black/Silver

text_fidelity_a:
ACPRO600 Good: Nice, minimal fit for my medium DSLR (canon 70d) with medium zoom lens (18-135) with lens hood on. Not too tight but not too much extra room. Seems to be well made. I like that it has a rain protector hidden in a lower pocket, but it'd be better if the case itself was weatherproof (is it that hard? Case Logic claims theirs is...)

Not so great: Pretty minimal pocket space outside the main compartment. Enough for a battery, a lens brush, memory. Not enough room for a lens blower, or other bulkier accessories. (Certainly no room for another lens, but you wouldn't want that in a holster.)

BAD: Strap. It's too short. I am not a big person (5'6"), and if you use it as a shoulder strap (isn't that how everyone uses it?) the camera will come nowhere near your hip. I have it adjusted to be as long as possible and still had to extend it with a couple of carabiners. That's ridiculous. Some reviews noted a well padded strap. Sort of. It has a sliding shoulder pad which is nicer than many. A little softer.
But it does slide around and I often find it's not on my shoulder after a while (the strap itself is just a basic nylon strap).

Maybe an issue? It'd be nice if the top of the bag was a bit wider. It takes me a little extra time to get the camera out because I have to squeeze my hand between the camera & bag. It's not tight - but just another 1/2" would be nice. That's going to vary with your camera.
Also, the bag doesn't let go when I lift the camera. The lens gets caught on the yellow camera support thingy a little bit, so I have to hold the bag with one hand while I pull the camera with the other. I suppose that's why gunslingers used to have a thong that tied the bottom of the holster to their thigh. That'd work - even if it looks a little silly...
text_fidelity_b: ACPRO600

text_fidelity_a:
Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Wireless Desktop Keyboard and Mouse - Black. Wireless , Comfortable, Ergonomic Keyboard and Mouse Combo with Split Design and Palm Rest. I'm a huge fan of Microsoft keyboards. Never been much of a fan of their office productivity software, but when it comes to keyboards, Microsoft fits my needs to a T. I'm using the Microsoft Digital Media Pro keyboard which (I believe) was discontinued years ago. A shame, since it has so many useful features.

But out with the old and in with the new. I tried and did not care for the previous generation of ergonomic split keyboards from Microsoft. At first glance the Sculpt looked to be a better design. The divide between the two sets of keys did not appear to be as pronounced, and my hands seemed to fit the keyboard very well. Love the feel of the pad on the wrist rest area!

Installation was straightforward, although getting the items out of the box was a challenge. I was happy to see that the necessary batteries were included - nothing worse than having to go hunt for batteries before you can start to use a new device.

The keyboard feel strongly reminded me of a laptop. For some, that may be a good feature. For me it is not. The flat keys and shorter throw makes typing feel "unnatural." I know that sounds vague, but it's the best way I can describe it.

This odd feel translated itself into a much slower typing speed - cut my throughput by about half. Since I write reports for a living, that's a rather big issue.

I also could not come to grips with the function key placement, size and meager supply of ancillary keys. That's a feature I love with my current Media Pro keyboard in that I can map pretty much any of the ample number of multimedia keys to any function I choose, or even a URL. For example, to start SPSS, Excel and WP I press one key. Another single keypress also opens my browser and my Amazon cart URL (and yes, the lettering on that particular key is pretty much worn completely off from use).

Still, if I was forced to, I could live with the keyboard. I could not, under any circumstances, live with the mouse in this set. Feels poor, lacks refinement, and far less versatile than my Logitech M500. I tried my best to get used to the Sculpt mouse, but just grew to hate it the longer I used it.

Now, my opinions are certainly affected by my current choices in keyboards and mice since I've been using them for years and years. I've changed PCs at least three times, but have retained the same keyboard and mouse since they have worked so well. If you have less keyboard/mouse "muscle memory" perhaps the Sculpt will fit the bill. The build quality seems decent, and if they are as reliable as other Microsoft keyboards, it will continue to work for some time. But for me, I just can't move the approval meter past "meh" for the keyboard and "dud" for the mouse. Three stars.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Wireless Desktop Keyboard and Mouse - Black. Wireless , Comfortable, Ergonomic Keyboard and Mouse Combo with Split Design and Palm Rest.

[Upgraded Version] Anker USB 3.0 SuperSpeed 10-Port Hub Including a BC 1.2 Charging Port with 60W (12V / 5A) Power Adapter [VIA VL812-B2 Chipset and Updated Firmware 9081] AH231 After having to practically rip the box to get this thing open, I set it up with my computer. The plug into the transformer is a little tight and I'm not sure it is entirely in. Though it's not moving. The computer did not recognize it at first. I do have a Sabrent 7 port hub plugged in to another USB slot on my laptop, but that is mostly filled with devices that are required for license verification (ilok, etc...) and it will only really take a powered hard drive even though it is powered.

Back to the Anker. I plugged in 2 Seagate 2 TB drives and a WD 2 TB drive, all bus powered. Once the computer finally recognized the Anker (I had to take the USB out and plug it back in) All three drives were quickly recognized. However after about 10 minutes I got a message that the last USB device I plugged in wasn't working and then the drives reconnected, except the WD This is the same behavior I was getting with my Sabrent that caused me to look for another hub. I was able to reconnect the WD by unplugging it a replugging it in. It is getting to be a very frustrating thing trying to find a USB 3.0 hub that can handle multiple drives.

I am running Windows 8 on an HP laptop. I will try this for a bit. I hope it doesn't have to go back because I had to damage the packaging to open it.

Update 12/2/16 - I've had this for 2 years. for the last year it has been a pain to use. The plug that was difficult to plug in now won't stay in. It turns off if I slightly move it. I'm looking for another one. Most of the spots are taken up by USB licensers, so when it stops working, it crashes my programs. very frustrating.
Updated 1/6/15: After keeping this plugged in, it is now working okay. I am not sure that some of the problems are not caused by my HP shutting the USB ports down as a power saver. I transferred a number of files from the WD to the Seagate using the Anker with no issues. It was actually very quick. However, I only had the 2 drives attached. I'm not sure there is anything out there that is any better. This is my 4th USB 3.0 hub I've tried and none of them really work well. And it could be my computer. But the whole point of a powered hub is that the computer doesn't have to support it.

7/16/16 Update
Still using this, but the plug doesn't like to stay in. I have to be very careful not to knock it out. Otherwise, it is still working well.
text_fidelity_b: [Upgraded Version] Anker USB 3.0 SuperSpeed 10-Port Hub Including a BC 1.2 Charging Port with 60W (12V / 5A) Power Adapter [VIA VL812-B2 Chipset and Updated Firmware 9081] AH231

text_fidelity_a:
Acer Aspire E 15 E5-575-33BM 15.6-Inch Full HD Notebook (Intel Core i3-7100U Processor 7th Generation , 4GB DDR4, 1TB 5400RPM Hard Drive, Intel HD Graphics 620, Windows 10 Home), Obsidian Black Definitely falls into the category of "you get what you pay for". This Intel Core i3-based laptop is astonishingly, agonizingly slow. I bought this to replace a 7 year-old MacBook Pro that had served well, but didn't have the horsepower to run the latest version of OS X. This Acer is only marginally faster than the MacBook, and feels slower in may respects. It's glacially sluggish to start-up or restart, and Excel and Word crawl along at speeds reminiscent of 1980s era PCs. Browser speeds - Chrome, IE, and the execrable Edge - all range from stagnant to plodding.

Other, more minor, negatives: the track pad might as well be 50 shades of gray, because it requires an extremely firm touch. The PC case is some form of black plastic that shows every fingerprint and smudge, all of which are impossible to remove.

I'm hoping for a day-after-Thanksgiving miracle deal to replace this cinder block of a PC.

Update 08.16.2017: Acer contacted me after this review was posted (big plus), and opened a case. They called me less than 24 hours after the case was opened (another big plus), but they had my laptop registered to someone else and I had to call them back when I had the laptop in front of me. The person I spoke with had me shutdown the laptop, and use a utility to reset system configurations to the default. When I restarted the computer, the performance had not improved. The support person commented that the laptop only has 4 GB of memory, which apparently makes it unsuited to running Excel. Acer sold the computer with this configuration, and no mention of not being able to run the MS Office suite (or open more than one tab on a browser). He then suggested wiping the computer and resetting it to the original state. I'm not willing to invest any more time in this laptop. Thanks to Acer for contacting me, but this one-star review stands. No more Acer products for me.

text_fidelity_a:
Tiffen 82VND 82 Millimeter Variable ND Filter I have one of the 77mm versions of this variable neutral density for cutting sunlight to manageable levels when shooting video outdoors. It works fine. I assume this 58mm version will work with typical Tiffen quality as well.

For those of you who might want to use it in conjunction with your factory lens hood, forget it.

The attaching thread is 58mm in diameter, but the outer diameter is 70.1 mm -- way bigger than the sunshade.

The front ring is threaded, but apparently only so the retaining ring can hold the front polarizer in place. The front thread measures out to 66.34mm to the inside of the thread (top of thread), or about 66.5 mm to the bottom of the thread groove. 67mm lens hoods exist and may fit, but not sure.

For my 77mm filter, I found a spare rubber lens shade that happened to be the same outer diameter as the filter and attached it with some electrician's tape. Works fine for longer lenses like the 70-200mm but vignettes on the 24mm end of the 24-70mm.

May need a matte box.

Comes in a very well built ballistic nylon pouch with Velcro closure and a very handy vinyl business card-sized window so you can label the thing and know what's inside.

It's a great filter that lets you shoot at 1/50 of a second at ISO 200 with the lens opened up to wider apertures to achieve shallow depth of field in bright sunlight. I find myself adjusting exposure by turning the filter a bit instead of changing f/stop.

Highly recommended. Just remember that you may be fighting flare unless you can rig up a sunshade, French flag or a matte box to keep the sun off it.

text_fidelity_a:
Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US) I was able to do a direct comparison between this and the SwissGear SA1908 ScanSmart Backpack. And it turns out that deciding which pack to grab on the way out is surprisingly one of the hardest decisions one could have to make. Both packs are obviously of the best quality with a similar nylon shell, strong stitching, and smooth zippers. Both are designed to fit 17" laptops and have similar interior volumes, and yet the features vary widely. Let's have a look at key points:

-The Targus is perfect for a user carrying a laptop and a tablet and/or Kindle. In front of the laptop compartment is a soft fabric lined pocket to hold a tablet against the laptop and protect the screen from scratches. The very front pocket is also soft with a piece of padding that fits the newest Kindle nicely.

-The SwissGear may be better for carrying just a laptop or two laptops. It has the ScanSmart feature, which is great when TSA allows it to work (sometimes they make you remove your computer anyway, either out of ignorance or their suspicion that you packed incorrectly for it to work - that makes it easier just to remove it sometimes rather than risk a fight with them). And I often store a second laptop in the ScanSmart opening.

-I love that on the Targus, the zipper pulls for the main compartment and the two side compartments can be placed between the bag and your back, thwarting casual thieves. As an extremely paranoid person, this gives extra peace of mind. For that matter, I really like the unique design of these pockets. The side pockets can be really useful, and the big compartment can be accessed from a larger opening. But that uniqueness comes at a cost...

-...and that cost is the looks. I didn't like the looks on the picture, but then it grew on me. In person, I don't really like it that much, but it might be growing on me. I guess the tradeoff is simple: you get a very unique design that works great and you get some serious padding for your electronics and some extra comfortable straps, but that all equals a slightly awkward looking pack. It's not too bad, but I think an accent color would go a long way. In contrast, the SwissGear under observation is quite beautiful and more traditional, yet not as padded or protected.

-The Targus came in a very thin box. It has a semi-rigid pad on the bottom that can fold up to flatten it out or fold down and attach with velcro to add some structure to the main compartment. This is also a very smart feature.

-The SwissGear has a phone/MP3 player holder with earphone exit, for those interested. That's not the best one I've ever seen though, as it is only a hanging cradle for the device.

-The Targus has more padding, while the SwissGear has a better airflow system for your back.

Conclusion: I really love both of these backpacks, and I'm surprised how different two top notch backpacks can be. I can see how the designers have to pick and choose the features they want to incorporate, because you really just can't have it all without making the pack bigger, and I wouldn't want that. They both deserve five stars, absolutely. The Targus strikes me as the pack for someone serious about the transportation and protection of their electronics, or anyone else who is intrigued to try this unique, excellent design.
text_fidelity_b: Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Wireless Headset for iPad, iPhone and iPod Touch Immediately, I realized I love these headphones. I'm not in love with the color, and I'm perplexed why companies always say something is for iPad, etc., although I suspect it is just the "cool" thing to do. I have no apple devices, but this worked immediately and perfectly for my Blackberry 9700, Xoom, and Win7 Laptop.

The first device pairs by itself, and devices 2-8 pair by holding 2 buttons for 5 seconds. After that, if multiple devices are turned on when you turn the headphones on, it seems to want to pick the first one you paired it with.

The BB picks it up as a Logitech Wireless Headset (not something generic), and you can then control the volume with the BB or with the headset itself (Did I mention the controls are all well positioned on the right headphone? - just two volume buttons, mic mute, micro USB charging port, and LED indicator), and you can also toggle between BB speaker phone and headset - they are obviously fully compatible - not generically. Pressing the mute button give you an audible cue, but does not change the BB display.

You'll never catch me in public with a normal bluetooth earpiece on anyway, so this is also great for calls at home - it will cancel out more background noise (because of the foam on both ears) so you can comfortably concentrate on your call. My tests show it working well more than the claimed 10m away (of course that partly depends on the other device's radio as well).

As another reviewer said, these sound good (and are capable of getting louder than I'll ever need), but are probably not as great as the full over-the-ear headsets. BUT, the wireless capability is really great to keep you fully uninhibited when exercising, cooking, or whatever you're doing when talking on the phone or listening to your music. For the record, I am 100% opposed to wireless shelf/tower speakers in a real home system, but this is a great solution for a headset.

Also, the mic backing out of the way is a must, so thankfully that is included. It not only pivots, but flexes toward or away from the mouth as well - very good design. Finally, the folding feature is great; any space saved is important. And the connecting wire connecting the two sides is accessible, if all that bending ever has it in need of a replacement.

Past helmet use has me thinking my skull is about as large as they come, and these are comfortable on me with the sides fully extended.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Wireless Headset for iPad, iPhone and iPod Touch

Skullcandy Crusher ANC Personalized Noise Canceling Wireless Headphone - Black Hands down the best headphones I've ever put on for bass. I ran them through my audio tester and these picked up way lower tones than my Senn's which have been my long standing pair for bass. Mid-range was true, sound was immersive, the headset was light and comfortable. A bit warm on the ears but pretty much all closed style headsets are.

OMG the constant never ending hissing. Unless you are playing something loud enough to cover it up, it is always there. Even when I turned off ANC, even when I switched to ambient mode. HIIIISSSSSSSSSSSSS. I tried to ignore it but it was always there. I work on the computer and sometimes I have to hear audio tracks and othertimes there is silence, I have to physically remove these every time I am not playing something or HIIIIISSSSSSSSSSSSSS. If you are like me and do not have sound coming out the entire time you are wearing them, do not buy. They will make you insane with rage, RAAWWRRR.

If you are only going to wear them while listening to music, and want the best bass you can find, buy these they are AMAZING for that, seriously. But ugh that hissing.

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz M1 in-Ear Noise Isolating Earphones While these don’t offer the sound quality of higher-end Brainwavz buds (or higher-end models from other brands), the sound quality and overall performance is quite good for the price point, and the comfort is excellent.

The best description I can offer of the sound quality is “clean.” The upper and mid ranges come through very clearly and are far more well-defined than typical with budget/value earbuds. The bass is not pronounced. It’s there, but it’s not what I’d describe as punchy. These are not an ideal set if you’re looking for head-thumping bass.

The comfort is typical for Brainwavz, which is to say it’s excellent. There’s a variety of ear tips so you can customize the fit to your ear. I’m especially fond of the Comply foam tips since they provide a great (but still comfortable) seal. That helps maintain good sound isolation and also helps with the bass response. It also helps keep the earbuds in place while exercising.

The cords are thin but seem sturdy enough for typical use. The same for the ear buds themselves. While they don’t have as solid of a build quality as higher-priced models, I don’t get the feeling that these will be falling apart anytime soon. That being said, it would have been nice to have more reinforcement where the cord meets the earbud, since that’s a prime stress point in use (even though these come with a very well made carry case, more often than not I just wind them around whatever device I am using).

For the price these are hard to beat. Highly recommend these as a not too expensive way to substantially upgrade from the stock earbuds that come with many devices.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz M1 in-Ear Noise Isolating Earphones

Sabrent 4 Port Portable USB 3.0 Hub for Ultra Book, MacBook Air, Windows 8 Tablet PC - Black (HB-RU34) This is a great choice if you need a USB hub but don’t have much room. It’s only 1.25 inches wide and 4.75 inches long. Very slim profile that makes it easy to fit onto a desk or next to a laptop.

The 4 USB 3.0 output ports are arranged along the top; the input port is on the end. As shipped, this is a passive port (e.g., no external power) but it does have a power input at the end for a DC 5V input. The power transformer needed is NOT included in the package. The only attachment included is a USB input cord.

There is an indicator LED to show it is receiving power. I didn’t have any problems using it with USB 3.0 and 2.0 devices. However, since it’s a passive hub, it’s not the best choice for really power-hungry devices, such as large external drives or for tasks such as charging a tablet. Those applications are better suited to a hub with an external power source.

The build quality seems very good. It’s plastic, but the case feels pretty durable. The ports are well-anchored and didn’t move when I stressed the input cables.

It’s well worth considering if you need a slim profile passive hub for USB 3.0 devices.
[Sample provided for review]

Philips SPP4105B/17 10-Outlet Home Office Surge Protector (Discontinued by Manufacturer) The outlets are spaced so that the larger plugs don't block multiple slots. There is plenty of room, even for the large ones.

Rather than trickling out power to devices that aren't on, the system automatically shuts down power to the energy saving outlet when the main outlet is shut off. This is great if the energy savers are peripherals and the main is a PC, but if you're doing something other than a computer setup it can be a pain to remember to only plug an "always on" device into this slot. If you shut that device off, everything in the 7 energy saving outlets will lose power. The power loss will trigger if you reboot your machine, which means that all of your peripherals will go through a full boot cycle as well.

I'd have preferred a switch to enable or disable this feature, and an outlet for charging USB devices rather than coax.

Rolling Spider I'm kind of them on this. It has its flaws no doubt, but it is a lot of fun.

The app you need is Free Flight 3. It doesn't say that anywhere in the instructions. There are training videos on YouTube that are helpful in figuring out how to use this. Definitely worth watching. The app itself is unintuitive and hard to use. Once you get used tip it, though it's pretty cool.

The drone can handle crashing into just about anything, and I know this because we were so bad at this we crashed it into just about everything except the cat. The cat didn't want to be in the same room with it. The blades can't break skin if you crash it into yourself. We had that happen too. The axle gets very hot from the friction though.

I like that is so tiny it can launch off your hand and fly or roll it indoors. I don't like the battery life. You get about five minutes of play time per charge. I like the appearance of the drone. It's very cute and comes with stickers.

Overall it's entertaining, but the battery life needs to improve before it's worth more than three stars.

The battery
text_fidelity_b: Rolling Spider

This is a small camera, only a little larger than a P&S. That's normally good. Except when the temperatures are in the teens (F). Even thin leather driving gloves are a bit clumsy, especially with the back panel buttons. I normally use fingerless mittens, but not this morning.
Edit:
I'm really liking this camera. My lens changing/handling skills are coming back after not being used for [cough] years. In terms of focal lengths, the basic kit lens (14-42mm) is good for 80% of shots. I'd wish for a couple of more f-stops, though.

Longer term: Still good. I have the F3 button set on MF. There are a few cases where the AF algorithm & I disagree. For some reason, buttercup yellow flowers have no inherent contrast & AF has a hard time seeing the details to focus. This brings up peaking & magnify & allows me to fine tune the focus.
I keep wishing for a 20-80 mm f/2.8 lens. Cheap, of course. ;)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Washable Wired Keyboard K310 I often eat at my desk, which is not the greatest thing. Croissant flakes, bits of cheese and even rice grains often find their way into the crevices of my standard keyboard at work. It gets really disgusting. A few times crumbs got stuck inside the keys and stopped them from working properly. I've used compressed air cans and mini vaccuums but they don't do that great a job. I often end up having to flip the thing over and give it a shake. In addition, I remove all the keys and use a Q-tip to wipe up dust and dirt that get encrusted in these tiny spaces, which is time-consuming.

So you can tell I was relieved to get this washable keyboard. This thing is made for the Oscar Madisons of the world (like me). While you can't use it underwater while scuba diving (the instructions say you shouldn't submerge it in more than 11" of water, and no more than 5 minutes at that), being able to do a wash and rinse (as if it were a dinner plate) is more than enough to get most dirt and crumbs out.

I also like the fact that there is no additional software to install - just plug into the standard USB port, wait a few minutes until your computer recognizes the hardware, and then you're off. The keyboard is about the same size as other computer keyboards, except that the keys feel more like ones you'd find on a laptop. They are round and smooth and make me feel I'm pushing buttons. Because they lay flatter on the surface of the keyboard, you get a softer sound when you type as opposed to the hardier tapping of regular keyboards.

It took me awhile to get used to the feel. The buttons lack the slightly concave ridges that keep your fingers nestled so my fingers felt slippery on them, but not enough to have a problem.

Despite these reservations, however, I think this is a well-made product that is very practical, especially for people like me, who'd rather write than clean. Now all I need is a washable mouse!
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Washable Wired Keyboard K310

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model I am director of a small publishing house. I've been using a $1,000 MacBook Pro 11.6 (Lion) laptop for over a year, with the Chrome browser, Gmail, and GoogleDrive as my online backup for laptop-based files of importance. I got accustomed to the trackpad (I switched the scrolling direction) and haven't used a mouse since I got my Mac. I do book production and cover design on it, sitting in the living room recliner (too far from an electrical outlet to use the adapter) but the battery runs down pretty quickly.

I wanted this Chromebook as a second machine for starting and ending my day: browsing and doing the cloud-based work I have to do, like accounting in Wave, managing social network-based marketing, ordering books, searching for cover art, reading manuscripts in Submittable, handling email, etc. My Mac with Adobe CS5 is essential for the actual book design and production, so I basically reserve its battery now for that.

What is amazing to me is how similar this Chromebook keyboard is to my MacBook Pro. The only time I realize I'm not on my Mac is when I hit what, on the Mac, is the caps lock key but on the Chromebook pops up apps. (There is no caps lock key on the Chromebook; supposedly you can press both shift keys at the same time to effect caps lock, but I guess I don't have the right touch because I can't get it to work.) Another slight difference is in how click and drag works; on the Chromebook, you hit the trackpad with your thumb, then drag.

Those who have already gotten accustomed to using Google-related commands for email, clearing the cache, and the like will be good to go without any learning curve. Chrome extensions and apps, of course, work as expected. (I am SO glad I had the prescience to realize a year ago that I definitely wanted to shift to a cloud-based approach!)

Now, a word about the quality of the monitor. I find the type on the screen to be MORE readable than on my Mac. It is much crisper and high-definition. The colors don't match between the two computers, but I'm not sure it's the Chromebook's fault. The Chromebook does seem to be able to sense how to adjust brightness based on the conditions of the room, which is helpful. Sometimes, however, my eyes start smarting, something that happens when I'm working on the Chromebook, but not on the MacBook Pro. I don't know what accounts for this. The sound is better on the Chromebook than on my Mac, especially if I use good headphones. When watching a movie, the color is a bit washed out compared to the really garishly brightly colored sets, but I prefer that.

I'm probably more of a power user when it comes to the user end of a computer, but I don't try to get in and hack things like some people do. Developer mode, need for static IP address, etc., I'm clueless about. But this is a well-built, fast, mostly no-fuss, low-cost and very light-weight piece of work with a long-lasting battery, which is exactly what I wanted. That I also got a seamless experience shifting from one machine to the other for a quarter of what my MacBook Pro cost? That's priceless!
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model

text_fidelity_a:
Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day PROS

1. It has 10 sockets/outlets.
2. Two of the sockets are offset from the other six. This allows them to be used for wide plugs, which is an important feature, because wide plugs are a frequent occurrence on appliances.
3. The color is an attractive but neutral black which makes the strip fade into the background more than the strips I own which are white or beige.
4. In addition to being a power strip, it also provides surge protection.
5. There are four USB ports that can be used for charging devices. One of them is a USB-C port and the other 3 are standard USB ports. The manufacturer claims in the manual that the three standard USB ports are “smart” USB ports.

CONS

1. I am not entirely comfortable trusting the “smart” USB ports on this device for charging. I feel more comfortable using a regular USB charging adapter and plugging it into a socket on the surge protector side of this device.

2. Regarding the smart USB ports, there are not adequate instructions either in the manual or on the manufacturer’s website that clearly explain the implications of this feature and how to utilize it. I cannot find information on the top mA it supports in charging.

GENERAL INFORMATION ON USB CHARGING

In order to test this device for my Vine review, I spent over two hours (!!!) trying to find comprehensible information on what the term “smart” means in the context of a USB port on a power strip like this one. Unfortunately, I was left with more questions than answers, for which hassle I’m dropping a star off this review. I’ve included some of what I learned below, for what it might be worth to any fellow Amazon customer who might be thinking of purchasing this product.

A smart USB charger port supposedly can, in and of itself, figure out what the optimal charging speed of a specific device is when it is plugged into that port, in order to neither overload it with too much current or under-deliver to it the optimal current. The question on everyone’s mind these days (it certainly has been on mine), is whether it is possible to destroy the battery in a particular device by slamming too much current into it. Apparently, the answer to this all-important question is: No. If, for example, you take a phone which comes with a 900mA wall charger, and you plug it into a 2,100mA charger that comes with a different device you own, it will not damage the phone. It will only speed up the length of time it takes for the phone’s battery to charge. However, if you have a USB device older than 2007, it may not charge on any USB ports newer than the (now ancient), 500mA USB 1.0 and 2.0 PC ports. Which means such older devices may not charge even on the “smart” USB ports on this device.

USB charging current is measured in mA (milliampere, 1/1000 of an ampere, the basic unit for measuring electrical current). There are three kinds of USB ports which are defined by their current specs: a standard downstream port, a charging downstream port, and a dedicated charging port. The first two are found on a desktop computer. The third kind is a “dumb” wall charger.

USB 1.0 and 2.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 500mA (0.5A).

USB 3.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 900mA (0.9A).

USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 ports can deliver between 1,500mA (1.5A) and 3,000mA (3A).

Charging downstream USB ports on a computer can deliver up to 1,500mA (1.5A).

Dedicated USB charging ports on a computer can deliver up to 3,000mA (3A).
text_fidelity_b: Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day

text_fidelity_a:
BRAINWAVZ S0 in-Ear Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones Clearwavz Remote & Microphone Stereo Headphone Headset for iPhone iPad, iPod & Android Devices (Black) I love how comfortable these ear buds are. I’ve always been pleased with Brainwavz earphone comfort, but these have raised the comfort bar even higher. I’m using it mainly with the tri-flange tips which I’ve tried with other headphones but didn't care that much for. With the S0's, however, the tri-flange fit very well, provide for good sound isolation, and stay put even when I’m on the treadmill. Very well done.

The sound quality is also quite pleasing. There’s ample bass without it being boomy or muddy. Just a nice, solid low-frequency response that sounds great. The mid-range is clear even at higher volumes. The only small shortfall is with the upper ranges, which are not as clear and sharp as they could be, and get somewhat shrill at high volumes. But at normal volumes it’s a nicely balanced sound, and considering the price, I would describe the sound quality as very good overall.

The build quality feels pretty solid. The cables are well-attached and have molded connectors at the ear buds to give it better durability. That’s important for me since, while this comes with a very nice carry case, I usually just wrap the cords around whatever device I’m using, which puts a lot of stress on the connectors. These feel more than solid enough to deal with that level of abuse. I have a few other Brainwavz earphones and have yet to have one fail on me.

This is well worth a spot on your short list if you’re shopping for a well-made, comfortable set of earbuds that deliver solid sound without breaking the bank. Highly recommend.

text_fidelity_a:
Symphonized Wired Earbuds with Microphone - Noise Isolating Headphones with Wire, Ear Buds with Wire, Headphones with Microphone for Computer, Corded Earbuds, Travel Headphones 3.5mm Graduation Gift Holy crap I like these! And I'm only on the 3rd of auditioning them! I got the red pair so they were only $21. Grab a pair and keep them as spares or give them to a friend who is listening to cheep buds.

No kidding while they may technically be 'better' I'd pick these to listen to over the ZR Carbon Tenor which were $40. I've been breaking in my Carbo Tenore for hours and hours and tip tuning to hope to like them move. This NRG are more musical and engaging. There is nice bass extension and bloom but there is still nice articulation. It's a bit much for me, but I'm buying them for someone who likes plenty of bass. The acoustic guitar sounds good, but not great (I play acoustic guitar). The carboTenore do a better job with an acoustic guitar, but there is nothing really wrong with how they handle the guitar.

They are not for people who like an upfront mid-range. Voices are a touched recessed. They lack a bit of chestiness in male vocals but not enough to be a fault (using Stevie Ray Vaughn to check). Just a sound signature thing. Female vocals sound good (using Annie Lennox to check)

While not much for soundstage there is some air around the instruments. They do an adequate job of capturing the room the instruments are played in. On both these counts, I like it more than on the Tenore. It's not a big difference but it's something I listen for when trying new phones.

I'm really excited to let these break in a bit (though they really don't need it) and do some tip tuning to tame the bass a bit to my liking. I'd rather EQ a bit of boom out than try to eq in some bass that is not there.

They do not need a lot of volume to sound good. (the Tenore need a bit of volume to sound their best

They are very comfortable to wear. Not too heavy, not too light and feel really balanced in the ear even though they stick out a bit. The shape makes them super easy to take in and out and the strain relief you can see in the picture means you don't have to be super careful of the cables.

I am super impressed with what I got for $22 dollars and plan to get a pair for myself at that price.
text_fidelity_b: Symphonized Wired Earbuds with Microphone - Noise Isolating Headphones with Wire, Ear Buds with Wire, Headphones with Microphone for Computer, Corded Earbuds, Travel Headphones 3.5mm Graduation Gift

text_fidelity_a:
WD Blue 1TB Mobile Hard Disk Drive - 5400 RPM SATA 6 Gb/s 9.5 MM 2.5 Inch - WD10JPVX I used this as an upgrade drive for the PS4. It caused one reboot on installing a lot of software over a slow Internet connection (it was during the upgrade of the software, and might have been caused by that) but it has been running flawlessly ever since.

It is stable, reliable, and quiet.

Don't let the speed be an issue here. Sony bullt at 5400 into the PS4 originally, so it will not need faster, and a faster drive could cause overheating. Two things to keep in mind when downloading the Sony firmware though. First, the folder names are case sensitive. PS4/UPDATE not ps4/update. If you are going to use this to upgrade the PS3, a thing to keep in mind when installing the system software is that the PS3 has trouble reading larger thumb drives. This nailed me when I tried a 120 gig drive. I had to roll back to an 8 gig, that did the trick.

For a laptop or netbook, I would favor a faster drive, but for the budget conscious, this one is excellent.
text_fidelity_b: WD Blue 1TB Mobile Hard Disk Drive - 5400 RPM SATA 6 Gb/s 9.5 MM 2.5 Inch - WD10JPVX

Panasonic HomeHawk Outdoor Wireless Smart Home Security Camera, Wide Angle View, Color Night Vision, 2-Way Talk, Works with Alexa & Google Assistant, 1 Camera Kit (KX-HN7001W) The Panasonic HomeHawk system has its good and its areas that could use some upgrades.
The good:
This is about as simple and install as you will get for a home monitoring system. No wires, five screws, charging the camera, downloading the app and you are ready to go, it is that simple. Once the cameras are charged and mounted I think it took me about 5 minutes to get everything running, and I am not technical by any stretch of the imagination.
The cameras are clear and provide good picture (you can select the quality of the picture when setting the system up) of the areas they are monitoring. Recordings are of good quality and clear, the night recording can be either color or black and white (infrared) depending on your choice.
Recording trigger areas can be set up along with sensitivity to movement in the recording area to trigger the recording to begin. All of these are very handy and easy to use.
The app is simple to use and pretty intuitive on how the system operates allowing almost everyone to use the system without any special knowledge. In all a good system for 95% of the people out there.
The things that can be improved.
It became apparent during setup of the outdoor camera (the one that looks like ET) that you need to mount it in a specific orientation, if you turn it over you cannot flip the image and everything will be upside down. If the ball neck for mounting the camera was just a little longer this would not be an issue as you could fit it under a soffit on your house wit a large field of view.
On the outdoor camera it works best when the rear of the camera is pointed in the direction of the base unit for connectivity. As you turn the camera and point the rear away from the base the signal drops pretty quick and the camera will not connect.
Other than these items the system is pretty easy to set up and use, now we see all the raccoons that show up to the house at night.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic HomeHawk Outdoor Wireless Smart Home Security Camera, Wide Angle View, Color Night Vision, 2-Way Talk, Works with Alexa & Google Assistant, 1 Camera Kit (KX-HN7001W)

Logitech Harmony 650 Infrared All in One Remote Control, Universal Remote Logitech, Programmable Remote (Silver) What can I say that hasn't been said by 6,200 previous buyers except that this Harmony 650 in silver is a great remote for a small single-remote system.

I'm using it on a patio with a TiVo, a Vizio 40" and an Amazon Basics SB20 sound bar. All three devices were easily found in the Harmony database and entered effortlessly into the remote using the MyHarmony app you download from Logitech to your laptop or desktop computer.

Having used the MyHarmony app to integrate my two Harmony Ultimate hubs for more complex remote IR systems that employ my network/router/phone as interfaces, I was already familiar with how Logitech has set up their software -- so it took only minutes to get the 650 into action.

Hint: before beginning to program your remote, gather the manufacturer and exact model number for each device you are going to control: TV, Amp, Sound Bar, Cable box, DVD player, Blu-ray Player, CD player, whatever. The MyHarmony software will ask you to add all the devices you are going to integrate. You'll need information from as many devices as you have current remotes for. When you're done, you put all the remotes away and use just the 650.

According to the MyHarmony app, the 650 can control 8 devices. I only needed to control three for my patio setup, so it was a simple process.

Bottom line, it's WAY easier to use a single Harmony 650 that to juggle three remotes (TiVo, Sound Bar and TV).

And after just a few minutes of easy online programming that then downloads to the 650 via a USB cable, I'm done.

As the 650 is being used on the patio outdoors, and subject to environmental attack from dust and moisture, I ordered the silicone cover for it. Works great: [[ASIN:B01N2SF2XX Harmony 650 Silicone Case for Logitech Harmony 650 700 Remote Controller Cover Anti Dust Anti-Slip]]
