text_fidelity_a:
Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black I lived and breathed full-sized Kensington trackball mice from about 1987 until my last one stopped functioning and I couldn't find them anymore...probably in the late '90s. Tried some others; all had small, lightweight balls that gave none of the feel and control of Kensinton's...Expert Mouse? Was that what it was called back then too? Because it was the same general design as the current Expert Mouse, but the body was computer-case white.

Anyway, I had several of those (the quality going downhill with each iteration, as I recall) and loved them, and since they disappeared (as far as I could tell), I adapted, first to trackpads, which I've never liked much, and then back to traditional mice which don't give nearly the control of a trackball. Now, at last, it seems Kensington has again begun to produce truly worthwhile trackball mice, and this is one. Oh, it's _so_ good to have one of these again.

I'm doing that thing I hate when other people do it and reviewing the product as soon as I've gotten it up and running, without any kind of experiential history behind my assessment. I'll come back and update this in the future if necessary. But so far: I'm happy, happy, happy to have a real, full-sized Kensington trackball mouse again, with a heavy, substantial ball. There are only two things about this device that I'm not crazy about: In my old Kensington mice, the ball rested on physical rollers and I could give the ball a good spin and it would keep spinning for a second before stopping; it spun much more freely in its cavity than this ball does (so far...maybe that's something that will break in?) [Update: yes, after about three days of use the ball rolls more smoothly and silently than the old one on rollers ever did]. And the other thing is the scrolling mechanism. It's weird. Despite the KensingtonWorks software trying to make us believe otherwise, the "scroll ring" itself actually has nothing to do with scrolling, nor with anything else - the "scroll ring" is not even a control, but just a static piece of chrome trim. What makes the mouse scroll is twisting the ball this way or that from the top, as if it were a knob. At first I thought the "scroll ring" wasn't working because I was trying to use it without touching the ball...which does nothing. And now that I've figured out how scrolling works (you rest your finger on the "scroll ring" and push and pull the side of the ball)...I'm not crazy about it. I'm getting used to it, but it's just a weird way to scroll (I can't for the life of me remember how I used to do it on the Expert Mouse decades ago). It does work though.

(Update on the scrolling: I'm also not crazy about the way the KensingtonWorks software handles the scrolling speed adjustment. When you make the base pointer movement speed faster, the pointer continues to move smoothly, but just faster. When you make the scrolling speed faster though, you lose all smoothness - the software makes the scrolling faster by breaking it into successively larger and more jarring jumps. At the slowest speed, it's pretty smooth; at the highest speeds it's no longer really scrolling, but simply jumping abruptly from one screenful (or page) to the next. Increasing the scrolling speed just increases the size of these jumps, but I find them jarring and annoying starting at the second or third lowest speed setting.)

I also had to figure out how to program one of the buttons as a click lock, since Kensington doesn't call it that anymore, but calls it "left drag", "right drag", and "middle drag" (and I have no idea what the difference is between those three - I just chose "left drag" and it's working fine).

So far, those are my only gripes, all minor. So happy to have one of these things again! =) (Did I mention that?)

Enjoy...
text_fidelity_b: Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black

Lasitu Portable Monitor 18.5 Inch 100Hz 100% sRGB FHD 1080P Travel Monitor IPS HDR USB C Portable Screen HDMI Gaming Monitor External Monitor for Laptop PC Phone Xbox PS4-5 Switch with Kickstand At the office, I had a dock and two large monitors in addition to my laptop screen. But in these days of COVID and work-from-home, I was stuck with just my little laptop screen. While my office offered to let me take my monitors home I just didn't have the space, and I do like to occasionally do work at the local cafe or lounge.

Enter this portable screen...

-It plugs into the laptop with just one cable and no separate power cable is needed! All I need to use it is the included USB-C cable and the screen itself!
-It's thin and its lightweight. In fact, it slides into my backpack's laptop pouch and still has room for both my laptop and my buttpad (for hard seating).
-It's perfect for travel since carrying an extra monitor is not possible... but you can literally take this anywhere with you.
-The protective cover doubles as a stand and works pretty well.

My only criticism would be that anytime it gets unplugged from the laptop, the settings reset, and when you plug it back in you have to readjust the settings. In my case, it defaults to level 20 brightness where I prefer it to be right at 80. It's only 4 button presses to change it which I have down now so its not a big deal but it would be nice if this setting was memorized somehow.

In the days of COVID and WFH, this has been one of the best productivity purchases I've made and it has been beyond worthwhile.

text_fidelity_a:
Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors) This jumpdrive is USB 3.0 (fast) but backward compatible with 2.0. It's a little cheesy looking because of its plastic "bubblegum" look, but the color-coding of the different size drives could be useful. I got the bright green 32 GB USB 3.0 stick for review, and when I put it into my USB port it showed installation files on the drive for both Windows and Mac. I double-clicked the Mac for my MacBook Pro, and it presented me with the installation screens. It was a little confusing how to get the software installed, and initially I had to install it on my computer to access the installation for just the flash drive; it's supposed to be optional to install it on your computer, but it wasn't apparent how to bypass computer installation. I had to delete my computer vault after it was created to get it off my computer.

Another confusion is that you are taken to a website with an offer for an Encryptstick software upgrade for a reduced cost or free for a 14-day trial. Apparently, all the best features of this device are not available if you just use the stick as a USB drive with the standard "Encryptstick Lite" app that comes with it. You will have AES encryption, but not the "military grade encryption," whatever that means. (The website lists the option to encrypt vaults with 128, 256, or 512-bit AES ciphers [1024-bit coming], registered and government approved, FIPS 140-2 compliant). Here are the other features listed on the website and, again, it's not clear which come with the standard installation and which with the upgraded one:

Runs on Multiple OS computers and all recently made USB flash drives
Encrypt & Decrypt Your Private Files
Easy to Use Encryption Interface [debatable!]
Speedy Auto-Updater
Lost Flash Drive Data Recovery Feature
Advanced Virtual Keyboard
Lock out Computer Installation is Optional - Not Essential
Lock out No Admin Rights Required
File Wipe Instant Lock
Quick Search, Live Search
Automatic Timeout
Limited Login Attempts
File Wipe File Shredder

I went on and purchased the upgrade (12.99 to Lexar users instead of the usual 39.99) because the advanced backup features are only available with the upgraded version and I did want them, but I thought it was a little sneaky how they presented all this. It's really not clear that you don't have to get the upgrade to make the stick itself work. Once you've purchased the upgrade, you are given links to download the upgrade for all versions (PC, Mac, and Linux) in an email.

Somehow I wound up with both the EncryptStick Lite and EncryptStick apps both running at the same time. I could not close out of either one of them, and attempting to eject the jumpdrive gave me an error saying I needed to close out of both apps. I had to force-quit the Lite app. That made me nervous about the whole thing.

I have to mention the following experience because, for me, it was an issue. The little lanyard (about the length of the drive when installed) is not attached when you take it out of the package, and I had a heck of a time getting it threaded through the end. The cord won't bend through the jumpdrive's hole, so it requires using an implement of some come to grasp the thread end and pull it through. My tweezers were too large, and so was the end of the large paperclip (all I had), so I wound up having to strip off the coating on an old bobby pin that I just happened to have lying in a drawer. Even then, I had to pop up part of the plastic cover on the front of the drive case a little to work the thread through, and I was worried about destroying the drive in the process. This whole process was very aggravating, so I think it would be better if they sold these with the lanyard already attached. Customers can then remove it if they don't want it, but I think the lanyard is quite useful. If you have more than one of these drives, you could hang them all up on a keyholder at your desk, then pull one off to take with you as needed.

Please note that I am downrating this product because of the initial confusion and hassles above, although in fairness this is not a good indication of the reliability and performance of the jumpdrive once the software and lanyard are installed. Consider this review to be of the initial experience with the jumpdrive and software. If I discover any more problems as I use this drive over time, I will come back and post them. For now, though, I'm tired of fooling with it!
text_fidelity_b: Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors)

Baseus USB-C Docking Station, USB C Data Hub Adapter with PD Type C Charging Port, 5-in-1 USB C Dongle Adapter for MacBook/Pro/Air 2018,Chromebook,XPS,Galaxy S10/S9/S8/Note9 This is a review for the Baseus 5-in-1 USB C Hub. I have a few different hubs now because Apple decided I only needed USB-C ports on my laptop. Depending on what I’m doing and how many devices I need to plug in, I’ll either use a hub or adapters.

WiFi signal strength can be impacted by hubs or similar devices, there’s some interference with USB 3.0 and 2.4Ghz networks. It’s a known problem, there’s a lot about it online if you’ve also run into it. I’ve noticed this using other hubs, and I have about the same degree of interference with this one.

I don’t love the design of this hub. I wish the hub’s USB-C plug was straight, not an “L.” While I can still plug in other USB-C things next to the hub, the “L” shape of the plug dictates how the hub sits on my desk.

The hub is bigger than it needs to be. Maybe if the glassy front was repurposed, the USB 3.0 ports laid out in a square rather than a line, it wouldn’t take up as much room on my desk. The big display only has a tiny icon to show me when the hub is on … I just don’t like the wasted space.
text_fidelity_b: Baseus USB-C Docking Station, USB C Data Hub Adapter with PD Type C Charging Port, 5-in-1 USB C Dongle Adapter for MacBook/Pro/Air 2018,Chromebook,XPS,Galaxy S10/S9/S8/Note9
